mainTopic: שמחת בית השואבה: songs, sayings, and feats of the Sages, the near-sleepless festival, and the fifteen שיר המעלות
overview: This amud continues describing שמחת בית השואבה from the משנה. The light was so bright that a woman could sort wheat by it. A ברייתא gives the songs of the חסידים and the בעלי תשובה, and the message both groups shared about תשובה. Next come sayings of הלל הזקן at the celebration, and his words to a floating skull about מדה כנגד מדה. רבי יוחנן teaches that a person's feet bring him where he is needed, and the story of שלמה's two scribes illustrates it. The גמרא then describes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל juggling torches and bowing in קידה. It discusses why לוי became lame, and lists other Sages who juggled. רבי יהושע בן חנניה says they hardly slept during the celebration, and the גמרא explains that they only dozed. Finally, רב חסדא discusses why דוד said the fifteen שיר המעלות, and the story of the rising תהום continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The light was bright enough to sort wheat
steps.stepSummary: The light of בית השואבה was so strong that a woman could sort wheat by it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman could sort wheat by the light of the בית השואבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes describing how bright the light of the celebration was. It gives a picture of that brightness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sorting wheat means picking out tiny stones and bad kernels, which needs good light. So this line shows the light was close to daylight. It expands on the משנה's statement that every courtyard in ירושלים was lit up.

keyTerms.meaning: the place of the water-drawing, where the סוכות celebration was held

phrases.english: A woman would sort wheat
by the light of the Place of the Water-Drawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִשָּׁה הָיְתָה בּוֹרֶרֶת חִטִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the elaboration on the משנה's description of the light, on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The light of שמחת בית השואבה was strong enough for fine sorting work.

steps.title: The song of the righteous: our youth did not shame our old age
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about the חסידים ואנשי מעשה, and a ברייתא says one group sang praise for a youth that did not shame their old age.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said 'the pious and men of action...'. The רבנן taught: some of them would say, 'Fortunate is our youth, which did not embarrass our old age.' These are the חסידים and men of action.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה and brings a ברייתא explaining what these people sang. This is the first of two groups.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only said that the חסידים ואנשי מעשה danced and sang. The ברייתא tells us the words of their song. This group lived righteously from youth, so they had nothing in their past to be ashamed of when they were old.

phrases.english: [The Mishnah said:] The pious and the men of action, etc.
The Rabbis taught: Some of them would say:
Fortunate is our youth
which did not embarrass our old age —
these are the pious and the men of action.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲסִידִים וְאַנְשֵׁי מַעֲשֶׂה כּוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חסידים sang praise for a youth free of sin, which left their old age with no shame.

steps.title: The song of the penitents: our old age atoned for our youth
steps.stepSummary: A second group sang praise for an old age that atoned for a sinful youth. These are the בעלי תשובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some of them would say, 'Fortunate is our old age, which atoned for our youth.' These are the penitents.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא describes a second group of singers. These were people who sinned when young and later did תשובה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה named only חסידים ואנשי מעשה, but the ברייתא shows that בעלי תשובה also sang at the celebration. Their song turns the first group's line around: the first group praised their youth, and this group praised their old age.

phrases.english: And some of them would say:
Fortunate is our old age, which atoned for our youth —
these are the penitents.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְיֵשׁ מֵהֶן אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second group, a mirror image of the first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The בעלי תשובה sang praise for an old age of תשובה that atoned for a sinful youth.

steps.title: Both groups' shared song
steps.stepSummary: Both groups sang together: fortunate is one who did not sin, and one who did sin should repent and be forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both these and those would say: 'Fortunate is one who did not sin. And one who sinned should repent, and He will forgive him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by giving the line that both groups sang together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each group praised its own path, and then both agreed on one message. Never sinning is best, but תשובה is always open and brings full forgiveness.

keyTerms.meaning: these and those, meaning both groups

steps.whatToRemember: At the celebration, both the lifelong righteous and the בעלי תשובה sang. Not sinning is best, and תשובה is always possible.

phrases.english: Both these and those say:
Fortunate is one who did not sin,
and one who sinned should repent, and He will forgive him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ אוֹמְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines the two groups' songs into one shared message.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Not sinning is ideal. One who sinned can repent and be forgiven.

steps.title: הלל: if I am here, everyone is here
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reports that הלל הזקן, while rejoicing at שמחת בית השואבה, said: if I am here, all is here; if I am not here, who is here?
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: They said about הלל הזקן that when he rejoiced at שמחת בית השואבה, he said: 'If I am here, everything is here; and if I am not here, who is here?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about what הלל הזקן said at the celebration.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply read, הלל meant that each person must act as if the obligation rests on him alone, and not rely on others to do it. Many מפרשים explain that הלל was speaking for כלל ישראל, or for God's presence, and not boasting about himself.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as הלל bragging. It is about personal responsibility, or it is said for the whole nation or for the שכינה.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל הִלֵּל הַזָּקֵן,
phrases.english: It was taught: They said about Hillel the Elder,
that when he was rejoicing at the Celebration of the Water-Drawing,
he said this:
If I am here — everyone is here,
and if I am not here — who is here?

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל הִלֵּל הַזָּקֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to another ברייתא about the celebration, this time about הלל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each person should act as if everything depends on him.

steps.title: הלל: my feet take me to the place I love
steps.stepSummary: הלל also said that his feet lead him to the place he loves, and God replies: if you come to My house, I will come to yours, and if not, I will not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would also say: 'To the place I love, there my feet lead me.' And God says: 'If you come to My house, I will come to your house. If you do not come to My house, I will not come to your house.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second saying of הלל about coming to the בית המקדש. It also gives God's answer to that coming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הלל says his love for the מקדש is what brings him there. Then God's reply works both ways: God's presence and blessing in our homes depend on our coming to His house.

phrases.english: He would also say this:
The place that I love —
there my feet take me.

phrases.aramaic: אִם תָּבֹא אֶל בֵּיתִי — אֲנִי אָבֹא אֶל בֵּיתֶךָ,
phrases.english: [God says:] If you come to My house — I will come to your house;

phrases.aramaic: אִם אַתָּה לֹא תָּבֹא אֶל בֵּיתִי —
phrases.english: if you do not come to My house —
I will not come to your house,

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another saying of הלל from the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coming to God's house brings God's presence and blessing to one's own home.

steps.title: Verse support: wherever My name is mentioned I will come and bless you
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק is brought to support God's promise to come to the person who comes to His house.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a פסוק from שמות as the source for the promise in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links God's 'coming to you and blessing you' to the place where His name is mentioned, which is the מקדש. This supports the idea that God comes to our house when we come to His.

keyTerms.meaning: as it is stated (introduces a פסוק)
I cause My name to be mentioned

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״בְּכׇל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי
phrases.english: as it is stated: “In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned
I will come to you and bless you” (Exodus 20:21).

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: בְּכׇל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק behind God's promise in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: God's promise to come to the house of whoever comes to His house.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמות כ:כא, 'בכל המקום אשר אזכיר את שמי אבוא אליך וברכתיך'.

steps.title: הלל and the floating skull: מדה כנגד מדה
steps.stepSummary: הלל saw a skull floating on the water and said: because you drowned others, they drowned you, and those who drowned you will be drowned.
steps.simpleTranslation: He also saw a skull floating on the water. He said to it: 'Because you drowned others, they drowned you. And those who drowned you will themselves be drowned.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another saying of הלל. This one is not about the celebration. It is about how God judges people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is מדה כנגד מדה: God punishes a person in the same way he sinned. Even the ones who carry out the punishment are judged in turn for what they did.
steps.confusionAlert: The Aramaic words come from the root טוף, meaning to float or drown. 'אטפוך' means they drowned you, and 'מטיפיך' means those who drowned you.

phrases.english: He too saw one skull
that was floating on the surface of the water,
he said to it:
Because you drowned [others], they drowned you,
and those who drowned you will be drowned.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף הוּא רָאָה גֻּלְגּוֹלֶת אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another saying of הלל, since the גמרא is already quoting him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God punishes מדה כנגד מדה, and those who carry out the punishment are judged as well.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known source for the principle of מדה כנגד מדה in how God runs the world.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: a person's feet bring him where he is needed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says a person's feet are responsible for him and bring him to the place where he is called for.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: 'A person's feet are guarantors for him. To the place where he is wanted, there they bring him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's saying because it connects to הלל's words about where his feet lead him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הלל spoke about feet going where a person loves to go. רבי יוחנן adds that feet also bring a person to the place God has decided he must be, even the place where he will die. The link between this step and הלל's saying is the idea of 'feet leading a person'.
steps.whatToRemember: A person's feet lead him: by choice to the place he loves (הלל), and by Heaven's decree to the place where he is needed (רבי יוחנן).

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

phrases.aramaic: רַגְלוֹהִי דְּבַר אִינִישׁ אִינּוּן עָרְבִין בֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: The feet of a person are guarantors for him;
to the place where he is demanded — there they lead him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: רַגְלוֹהִי דְּבַר אִינִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connected by topic to הלל's saying about feet in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person's feet bring him to the place where Heaven has decided he must be.

steps.title: שלמה tries to save his two scribes from the מלאך המות
steps.stepSummary: The מלאך המות is sad because he must take שלמה's two scribes. שלמה sends them to לוז to save them, but they die as soon as they arrive.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two Cushite scribes who served שלמה, named אליחורף and אחיה. One day שלמה saw the מלאך המות looking sad and asked him why. He answered that he had been told to take the lives of these two men. שלמה had demons carry them to the district of לוז, where the מלאך המות normally has no power. But the moment they arrived in לוז, they died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that illustrates רבי יוחנן's teaching from step 9, that a person's feet bring him to where he is meant to be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שלמה tried to protect his scribes by sending them to the one place where people do not die. The surprise ending is that they died there anyway. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: The district of לוז, a place where the מלאך המות has no power

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume שלמה's plan simply failed by bad luck. The point of the story, explained in the next step, is that his plan is exactly what brought them to their destined place.

phrases.english: Those two Cushites
who would stand before Solomon,
Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha,
they were Solomon's scribes.
One day he saw the Angel of Death
and he was sad.
He said to him: Why are you sad?
He said to him: Because they are demanding from me
these two Cushites who are sitting here.
phrases.notes: He has been ordered to take their lives.

phrases.english: He handed them over to the demons,
and sent them to the district of Luz.
When they reached the district of Luz, they died.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ תַּרְתֵּי כּוּשָׁאֵי דַּהֲווֹ קָיְימִי קַמֵּי שְׁלֹמֹה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that illustrates רבי יוחנן's statement about a person's feet.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שלמה sent the scribes to לוז to escape death, and they died upon arriving.

steps.title: The מלאך המות explains why he is now happy
steps.stepSummary: The next day the מלאך המות is happy. He explains that he had been told to take the scribes in לוז, and שלמה himself sent them there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next day שלמה saw the מלאך המות looking happy and asked him why. He answered: the exact place where I was told to take them is the place you sent them.
steps.whatsHappening: The story reaches its twist. The מלאך המות explains that שלמה's rescue plan is what brought the scribes to their place of death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The order was for them to die specifically in לוז. Because they never went there, the מלאך המות was stuck, and that was why he was sad. שלמה's attempt to save them is what carried out the decree.

phrases.english: The next day, he saw the Angel of Death
and he was happy!
He said to him: Why are you happy?
He said to him: The place where they demanded them from me,
that is where you sent them.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִמְחַר, חַזְיֵהּ מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת דַּהֲוָה קָבָדַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the surprise ending of step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The scribes were destined to die in לוז, and שלמה's act brought them there.

steps.title: שלמה declares that a person's feet lead him to his destined place
steps.stepSummary: שלמה draws the lesson: a person's feet are responsible for him and bring him to the place where he is called for.
steps.simpleTranslation: Right away שלמה said: a person's feet are his guarantors. They bring him to the place where he is called for.
steps.whatsHappening: שלמה states the moral of the story. It is the same idea רבי יוחנן said in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows that you cannot escape the place you are destined for, because your own movements take you there. This closes the story and connects it back to רבי יוחנן's statement.

keyTerms.meaning: Where he is called for, demanded

steps.whatToRemember: A person's feet bring him to his destined place. שלמה tried to save his scribes, and his plan is what brought them to it.

phrases.english: Immediately Solomon began and said:
The feet of a person
are responsible for him;
to the place where he is demanded,
there they lead him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיָּד פָּתַח שְׁלֹמֹה וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the moral of the story in steps 10-11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A person's feet bring him to the place where he is destined to be, which matches רבי יוחנן in step 9.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל juggles eight torches
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל would juggle eight flaming torches at שמחת בית השואבה without them touching each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: they said about רבן שמעון בן גמליאל that when he rejoiced at שמחת בית השואבה, he would take eight flaming torches. He would throw one and catch one, and they never touched each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the topic of שמחת בית השואבה. It brings a ברייתא describing the amazing way רבן שמעון בן גמליאל celebrated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds another example of how great people rejoiced at this celebration, like הלל in step 5. The point is the great skill and joy he put into the celebration.

keyTerms.meaning: The celebration of the water-drawing on סוכות

phrases.english: It is taught in a baraita: They said about him,
about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
that when he would rejoice at the Celebration of the Water-Drawing,

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה נוֹטֵל שְׁמֹנֶה אֲבוּקוֹת שֶׁל אוֹר,
phrases.english: he would take eight flaming torches,
and throw one and catch one,
and they would not touch each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא: אָמְרוּ עָלָיו עַל רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story about feet and returns to the theme of שמחת בית השואבה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל juggled eight torches at שמחת בית השואבה.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's special bow called קידה
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא describes his bow: thumbs pressed into the ground, kissing the floor, and straightening up. Nobody else could do it, and this bow is called קידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he bowed, he would press his two thumbs into the ground, bend down, kiss the floor, and straighten up again. No other person could do this. This is the bow called קידה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a second amazing feat of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and it defines the word קידה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קידה is an extremely difficult bow, balanced only on the thumbs. Defining it here sets up the next story about לוי, who tried to perform it.

keyTerms.meaning: A special, very difficult form of bowing

phrases.english: And when he would bow down,
he would press his two thumbs into the ground
and bend, and kiss the floor, and straighten up,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין כׇּל בְּרִיָּה יְכוֹלָה לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן,
phrases.english: and no other creature could do this,
and this is kidda.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְשֶׁהוּא מִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה, נוֹעֵץ שְׁנֵי גּוּדָלָיו בָּאָרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with his second feat and defines קידה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קידה is bowing on the thumbs, kissing the floor, and straightening up.

steps.title: לוי demonstrates קידה and becomes lame
steps.stepSummary: לוי showed רבי how קידה is done and became lame.
steps.simpleTranslation: לוי demonstrated the קידה bow in front of רבי, and he became lame.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story showing how hard קידה is. Even the great לוי was hurt trying it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows that קידה was dangerous even for a great חכם. It also sets up the next step, where the גמרא questions whether the bow was really what made him lame.

phrases.english: Levi demonstrated kidda
before Rabbi, and became lame.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵוִי אַחְוִי קִידָּה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells what happened when someone else tried the קידה just described.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לוי became lame after demonstrating קידה.

steps.title: Challenge: רבי אלעזר says לוי became lame for a different reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the bow really caused it. רבי אלעזר said לוי became lame because he spoke harshly toward Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: Was that really what caused it? But רבי אלעזר said: a person should never speak harshly toward Heaven, because a great man once spoke harshly toward Heaven and became lame. Who was he? לוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 15. It quotes רבי אלעזר, who gives a different reason for לוי's lameness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 says the קידה made לוי lame. רבי אלעזר says it was a punishment for speaking harshly to ה׳. These look like two competing explanations for the same injury.

phrases.english: And did that cause it for him?
But didn't Rabbi Elazar say:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם אַל יָטִיחַ אָדָם דְּבָרִים כְּלַפֵּי מַעְלָה,
phrases.english: A person should never speak impertinently toward Heaven,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֲרֵי אָדָם גָּדוֹל הֵטִיחַ דְּבָרִים כְּלַפֵּי מַעְלָה
phrases.english: for a great person spoke impertinently toward Heaven
and became lame; and who was he? Levi.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא גְּרַמָא לֵיהּ? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the cause of the lameness given in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 15 that the קידה caused לוי's lameness.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר says the lameness was a punishment for speaking harshly toward Heaven, which seems to contradict blaming the bow.

steps.title: Answer: both causes worked together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that both caused it. The harsh words made him vulnerable, and the bow is when the injury happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: This and that both caused it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by saying there is no contradiction. Both reasons are true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Speaking harshly toward Heaven was the deeper reason, and the קידה was the event through which the punishment came. Because of his words, he was hurt while straining to do the bow.
steps.whatToRemember: לוי's lameness had two causes. Speaking harshly toward Heaven was the reason, and the קידה was the moment it happened.

phrases.english: This and that both caused it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא וְהָא גְּרַמָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The bow and the harsh words seemed to be two competing explanations.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are true. The harsh words caused the punishment, and it happened during the bow.

steps.title: Sages who juggled to bring joy
steps.stepSummary: After the story of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל juggling torches, the גמרא lists other Sages who juggled: לוי with eight knives, שמואל with eight cups of wine, and אביי with eight (or four) eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: לוי would juggle eight knives in front of רבי. שמואל would juggle eight cups of wine in front of King שבור. אביי would juggle eight eggs in front of רבה, and some say four eggs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the theme of juggling torches by listing other great Sages who juggled to honor and gladden others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These stories show that even the greatest Sages did playful-looking feats to create joy for a great person or a מצוה. The ending, 'some say four eggs,' is simply a different version of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: juggling, tossing items up and catching them

phrases.english: Levi would juggle before Rabbi
with eight knives.
Shmuel, before King Shapur,
phrases.notes: שבור was the Persian king, who was friendly with שמואל.

phrases.english: with eight cups of wine.
Abaye, before Rabba, with eight eggs,
and some say with four eggs.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵוִי הֲוָה מְטַיֵּיל קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of juggling from רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's torch juggling (Step 13), and features the same לוי from Steps 15–17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Great Sages performed juggling feats to bring honor and joy.

steps.title: No sleep during the Water-Drawing celebration
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי יהושע בן חנניה: during שמחת בית השואבה, 'we did not see sleep in our eyes.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי יהושע בן חנניה said, 'When we celebrated שמחת בית השואבה, we did not see sleep in our eyes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא in which רבי יהושע בן חנניה describes, from his own experience, how intense the celebration was: they did not sleep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a strong claim: no sleep for the whole festival. It sets up two later moves. First the ברייתא explains the schedule (Step 20). Then the גמרא challenges whether this is even possible (Step 21).

keyTerms.meaning: The celebration of the water-drawing on סוכות
We did not see sleep in our eyes

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya said:
When we would rejoice in the Celebration of the Water-Drawing,
we did not see sleep in our eyes.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the juggling stories to a new ברייתא about how intense the celebration was.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During שמחת בית השואבה, the celebrants did not sleep.

steps.title: The full day's schedule
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains how they had no time to sleep. It lists their schedule from the morning תמיד through prayers, קרבנות, learning, meals, מנחה, and the afternoon תמיד, and then the celebration all night.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? In the first hour, the morning תמיד. From there to תפילה, then to the מוסף offering, then to תפילת מוסף, then to the בית המדרש, then to eating and drinking, then to תפילת מנחה, then to the afternoon תמיד, and from then on to שמחת בית השואבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question 'כיצד' (how so?) by walking through a packed day that leaves no room for sleep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The day was full of מצוות from morning to evening, and the night was spent celebrating. So there was simply no free slot for sleep. This is still part of the same ברייתא, not a new voice.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? (the source explains its own statement)

phrases.english: How so?
The first hour: the morning daily offering;
from there to prayer;
from there to the additional offering;
from there to the Musaf prayer;
from there to the study hall;
from there to eating and drinking;
from there to the afternoon prayer;
from there to the afternoon daily offering;
from here onward, to the Celebration of the Water-Drawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד? שָׁעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה תָּמִיד שֶׁל שַׁחַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the claim of Step 19 by showing the schedule that left no time for sleep.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The day was filled with מצוות and the night with celebration, so there was no time to sleep.

steps.title: Is it possible to go days without sleep?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא with רבי יוחנן's rule: someone who swears not to sleep for three days gets מלקות for a שבועת שוא, and he may sleep right away, because such a vow is impossible to keep.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? But רבי יוחנן said: if someone swears, 'I will not sleep for three days,' we give him lashes, and he may sleep immediately!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions whether רבי יהושע בן חנניה could really mean they did not sleep at all, since רבי יוחנן says no person can stay awake for three days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן treats an oath not to sleep for three days as a שבועת שוא, an oath that is impossible to keep. It is so impossible that the person is punished right away. So how could people go a whole week of the festival without sleep?
steps.confusionAlert: He is not punished for sleeping. He is punished for making a false, impossible oath (a שבועת שוא), and that is exactly why he is allowed to sleep right away.

phrases.english: Is that so? But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
'An oath that I will not sleep for three days' —
we flog him, and he sleeps immediately!
phrases.notes: The oath is a שבועת שוא because it cannot be kept.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the literal reading of Step 19's claim of no sleep.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע בן חנניה's statement 'לא ראינו שינה בעינינו'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן rules that three days without sleep is impossible, so a whole festival without sleep cannot be literally true.

steps.title: They only dozed on each other's shoulders
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reinterprets the ברייתא: they did not have real, proper sleep. They only dozed while leaning on each other's shoulders.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what he means: we did not taste the taste of real sleep, because they would doze on each other's shoulders.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by explaining that 'no sleep' means no proper sleep. They still napped a little while leaning on one another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'did not see sleep' are read as 'did not taste real sleep.' Dozing counts as some rest, so there is no conflict with רבי יוחנן. The celebration is still shown to be very intense.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is what he means

steps.whatToRemember: 'We did not see sleep' does not mean zero sleep. It means no real sleep. They only dozed on each other's shoulders, which fits רבי יוחנן's rule that a person cannot go three days without sleep.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what he is saying:
we did not taste the taste of sleep,
because they would doze on each other's shoulders.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves Step 21 by reinterpreting the wording of Step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'We did not see sleep' meant no sleep at all, which is impossible according to רבי יוחנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means no proper sleep. They dozed on each other's shoulders.

steps.title: Why did דוד say fifteen שיר המעלות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's 'fifteen steps.' רב חסדא asks a Sage who arranged אגדה for him: what do David's fifteen שיר המעלות correspond to?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Fifteen steps.' רב חסדא said to a certain Sage who was arranging אגדה before him: Did you hear what these fifteen מעלות correspond to? Why did דוד say them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new phrase in the משנה, the fifteen steps, and sets up a question about the fifteen שיר המעלות in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה linked the fifteen steps in the בית המקדש to the fifteen שיר המעלות. רב חסדא wants to know what event led דוד to compose exactly fifteen. This question sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Fifteen steps / fifteen Songs of Ascents

phrases.english: 'Fifteen steps.'
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, opening a new topic.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְהָהוּא מִדְּרַבָּנַן
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said to a certain one of the Sages
who was arranging aggada before him,
he said to him: Have you heard
regarding these fifteen Songs of Ascents,
corresponding to what did David say them?

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מַעֲלוֹת. אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְהָהוּא מִדְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the sleep discussion and opens a new topic from the next phrase in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What event the fifteen שיר המעלות correspond to

steps.title: The תהום rose when דוד dug the שיתין
steps.stepSummary: The Sage answers in the name of רבי יוחנן: when דוד dug the שיתין, the תהום rose up and threatened to flood the world. דוד said the fifteen מעלות and brought the waters down.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: רבי יוחנן said this: when דוד dug the שיתין, the deep rose up and wanted to flood the world. דוד said the fifteen מעלות and brought it down.
steps.whatsHappening: The Sage answers רב חסדא's question with a story from רבי יוחנן about why the fifteen songs were said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fifteen songs were said in response to a danger: the waters of the deep rising. Through these songs דוד made the waters go back down. This answer immediately prompts a wording problem, which comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The deep pits/drains under the מזבח

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: So said Rabbi Yochanan:
At the time David dug the drainage pits,
the deep rose and sought to flood the world.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר דָּוִד חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מַעֲלוֹת וְהוֹרִידָן.
phrases.english: David said fifteen Songs of Ascents and brought them down.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's question from Step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fifteen songs correspond to the event when the deep rose as דוד dug the שיתין, and the songs brought the waters down.

steps.title: Then they should be called 'descents'
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא challenges the answer: if the songs brought the waters down, they should be named 'Songs of Descents,' not 'Songs of Ascents.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why 'fifteen Ascents'? It should have said 'Descents'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא points out that the story does not match the name. Songs that brought waters down should not be called 'ascents.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name מעלות means going up, but the story describes the waters going down. This mismatch challenges the answer. The resolution comes next.

phrases.english: If so,
fifteen 'Ascents'?
It should have said 'Descents'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה ״מַעֲלוֹת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 24 because it does not match the name of the songs.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's explanation that the songs brought the waters down
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Songs that caused waters to descend should be called 'יורדות', not 'מעלות'.

steps.title: רב חסדא gives the correct version of the story
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא answers his own challenge by retelling the story the way it was originally taught. He starts with the same opening: when דוד dug the שיתין, the תהום rose and threatened to flood the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to him: Since you reminded me of this matter, this is how it was actually taught: At the time that דוד dug the שיתין, the waters of the deep rose up and wanted to flood the world.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא now gives what he says is the correct version of the story. This sets up the fix to his own question about the name 'Songs of Ascents.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening of the story stays the same: the שיתין were dug, and the תהום rose up. The real change will come in how דוד handles the waters. In the full corrected version, the fifteen songs are the thing that brings the waters back up, so the name 'Ascents' fits.

keyTerms.meaning: This is how it was taught (the accurate version)
To wash it away; to flood it

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רב חסדא is telling a brand-new story. It is the same story, and he is correcting how it goes. The beginning matches what the Sage said, and the difference comes later.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern in the גמרא: a Sage fixes a reported tradition by giving its accurate wording. Here the correction removes the problem with the name 'Ascents.'

phrases.english: He (Rav Chisda) said to him: Since you reminded me (of the matter),
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets (מִלְּתָא). רב חסדא now remembers the correct tradition.

phrases.english: this is how it was stated:
phrases.notes: Here comes the correct version of the teaching.

phrases.english: At the time that David dug the drainpipes (the deep pits under the altar),
the waters of the deep rose up
and sought to flood the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הוֹאִיל וְאַדְכַּרְתַּן מִלְּתָא, הָכִי אִתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's own challenge from Step 25 by giving the correct version of the tradition from Step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual correction: the tradition was reported inaccurately, and the original version is restored.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fifteen songs pushed the waters down, so they should be called 'Songs of Descents.'
steps.terutzMaskana: In the accurate version, the songs are connected to bringing the waters up, which fits the name 'Ascents.' The full corrected story finishes on the next amud: the waters sank too far, and דוד said the fifteen songs to raise them back up.

steps.title: דוד asks whether he may write God's Name
steps.stepSummary: With the world in danger of flooding, דוד asks if anyone knows whether it is permitted to write the שם. His question continues into the next passage.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד said: Is there anyone who knows whether it is permitted to write the Name (of God)...
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the story, דוד asks a הלכה question: may he write God's Holy Name to stop the flood? The question is not finished here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Writing God's Name on something that might be erased or thrown away is normally a serious problem. דוד wants to use the Name to hold back the waters, but first he wants to know whether that is allowed. The rest of his question (writing it on a clay shard and throwing it into the deep) comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The Name, meaning God's Holy Name

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is cut off at the end of the amud. The word שֵׁם is not the end of דוד's question. Keep reading on the next amud to see what he wanted to do with the Name.

phrases.english: David said:
Is there anyone who knows
whether it is permitted to write the (sacred) Name
phrases.notes: The question continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר דָּוִד: מִי אִיכָּא דְּיָדַע אִי שְׁרֵי לְמִכְתַּב שֵׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the corrected story from Step 26. Facing the flood, דוד looks for a solution and raises a הלכה question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether it is permitted to write God's Holy Name for use in stopping the rising תהום. The details are completed on the next amud.
